sec.title: Background
sec.p: The potential benefits and risks of combination therapy with sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) versus monotherapy remain a subject of debate to optimize metabolic and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. This study aims to systematically review and meta-analyze the available evidence from randomized controlled trials.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A comprehensive search identified relevant randomized controlled trials comparing combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA to monotherapy or treatment as usual (TAU). The main outcome was the incidence of hospitalization for heart failure. Other outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, stroke, and myocardial infarction), changes in metabolic parameters, and adverse events. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated risk ratios (RRs), mean difference (MD), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We assessed the risk of bias in included studies using the Cochrane ROB 2.0 tool.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The meta-analysis included 10 randomized controlled trials with 42,651 participants, of which 2,820 were on combination therapy and the rest on SGLT-2i (37.1%), GLP-1RA (20.1%) monotherapies or TAU (42.8%). Combination therapy had a lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure versus GLP-1RA monotherapy (RR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.22; 0.65), SGLT-2i monotherapy (RR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.19; 0.75), and TAU (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.24; 0.75), respectively. Combination therapy also had a significantly lower risk of MACE versus TAU (RR = 0.73, 95% CI 0.61; 0.88). Combination therapy showed greater weight loss and hemoglobin A1c reduction versus SGLT-2i monotherapy (MD = -2.20, 95% CI −3.09; −1.31 and MD = −0.74, 95% CI −1.21; −0.27), respectively, while no difference was noted versus GLP-1RA monotherapy. The incidence of nausea and diarrhea was higher with combination therapy versus SGLT-2i monotherapy (MD = 3.34, 95% CI 1.74; 6.43 and MD = 1.75, 95% CI 1.10; 2.77), respectively.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA may provide superior cardiovascular, weight, and Hemoglobin A1c outcomes versus monotherapy despite higher gastrointestinal adverse events. These results may impact the management of patients with metabolic and cardiovascular diseases and highlight the need for further research on combination therapy to optimize outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) represents the primary cause of mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [1].

Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) provide cardiorenal benefits, and reduction in weight, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and systolic blood pressure, through various mechanisms involving nutrient-sensing pathways [2, 3]. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) enhance cardiometabolic health, leading to improved glycemic control, weight loss, and better cardiovascular risk profile [4]. A review by Green et al. highlighted that SGLT2i significantly lower the risk of cardiovascular disease-related death, renal complications, and hospitalization for heart failure and end-stage renal disease in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), respectively [5]. In addition, large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and previous meta-analyses demonstrate that GLP-1RAs reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and stroke, and also decrease the risk of hospitalization due to heart failure in patients with T2DM [6–8].

Previous RCTs showed that combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA may have added value compared to monotherapy in terms of cardiometabolic effects such as body weight, HbA1c, and blood pressure [9–11]. In another study, a 12-week combination therapy showed greater vascular and myocardial function improvement, particularly in those with impaired left ventricular (LV) function [12]. The synergistic or additive cardiovascular benefits observed with the combination of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA are attributed to these two drug classes' complementary mechanisms of action. GLP-1RA has been shown to exhibit anti-atherogenic and anti-inflammatory effects, while SGLT-2i modulates vascular hemodynamics. Current guidelines, such as those from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), recommend the use of SGLT-2i as a first-line treatment in patients with T2DM with multiple atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors, established ASCVD, patients with T2DM and HFrEF to reduce the risk of heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death [13]. Additionally, GLP-1RA is also recommended for patients with T2DM at risk of with heart failure. The American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines suggest the initiation of SGLT-2i or GLP-1RA in patients with T2DM who have additional cardiovascular risk factors [14]. The European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD 2022) also recommends SGLT-2is and GLP-1RA independent of metformin use in patients with high-risk of ASCVD, heart failure, and CKD [15].

However, the combined use of GLP-1RA and SGLT-2i may increase the total cost of medical care and potentially lead to a higher prevalence of medication-related adverse events [16, 17]. Thus, a systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in this study in order to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA compared to monotherapy of each individual drug in patients with T2DM.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines for reporting [18]. The study is registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (ID: CRD42024546051). Two independent reviewers performed a comprehensive literature search on the PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus databases from inception to April 18, 2024, without language restriction. Supplementary search techniques (e.g., Google Scholar, citation searching, etc.) were employed to ensure no publication was overlooked during the literature search process.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: K.H. guided the search strategy, and A.M. and S.S. performed the systematic search using specific keywords and Medical Subject Headings. Further details are available in Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Following the systematic literature search, all citations from each database were imported into the Rayyan Intelligent Systematic Review web application (www.rayyan.ai, Rayyan Systems Inc. Software Development. Cambridge, MA) [19]. The application was utilized to resolve any potential duplicates. After conducting an initial screening, two reviewers (A.M. and S.S.) worked independently to assess the titles and abstracts of the studies to determine whether they met the inclusion criteria. Studies that were deemed potentially relevant were then screened in full text by the same reviewers. Those studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria were subsequently excluded.

This study included randomized clinical trials that evaluated the cardiometabolic effectiveness and safety of the combination therapy of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RAs versus monotherapy with either SGLT-2i, GLP-1RA, or treatment as usual (TAU) in adults (≥ 18 years) with T2DM. The term TAU encompasses various definitions mentioned in the included studies, which include placebo intervention, low-calorie diets, and patients awaiting bariatric surgery who undergoing caloric restriction. Given that our study aims to evaluate the effects of SGLT2i and GLP-1RA, and considering that these TAU definitions do not include diabetes mellitus treatments that could introduce bias into our results, we have collectively categorized all these variations under the term TAU for consistency in our analysis. There was no limitation on the baseline treatments. Exclusion criteria for our study were: (1) no RCT design; (2) no arm dedicated to the combination therapy of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RAs; (3) lack of a control arm; (4) incomplete studies; (5) not full-text publication in English; (6) studies for which full-text access was not available; and (7) studies without diabetic population.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: The data extracted from each study included information on the first author, publication year, country, criteria for inclusion and exclusion, follow-up duration, baseline characteristics of participants, drug history, lab data, treatment characteristics, and outcomes. The main outcome was hospitalization for heart failure and other outcomes were MACE outcomes (cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and all-cause mortality), metabolic outcomes (changes in HbA1c, weight, fasting plasma glucose (FPG)), and safety outcomes (severe adverse events, nausea, diarrhea, severe hypoglycemia, urinary tract infection, adverse events-related discontinuation). Data extraction for the systematic review was performed by two independent reviewers (A.M. and S.S.).

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The included studies were assessed for quality using version 2 of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) [20]. RoB 2 assesses five domains to determine the risk of bias in randomized controlled trials: the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. The risk of bias was evaluated by two reviewers (A.M. and D.S.) independently, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion with a senior (KH). If necessary, the third reviewer was consulted for further clarification. The certainty of results was assessed by using “GRADE and quality of evidence system” [21]. In this system, the quality of systematic reviews included RCTs set to be high and downgraded by 5 criteria assessment: (1) risk of bias in individual studies, (2) inconsistency of results between studies, (3) indirectness of evidence, (4) imprecision, and (5) publication bias.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: In this systematic review, continuous outcome variables were assessed using mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). However, dichotomous outcomes, such as cardiovascular outcomes and safety outcomes, were analyzed using risk ratio (RRs) with 95% CIs. When standard deviations (SDs) were not provided in studies, they were estimated from the reported standard errors (SEs) or the CIs that were given. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. In studies with multiple treatment arms, including combination therapies and monotherapies with either SGLT-2i, GLP-1RA, or TAU, we restructured these into separate comparisons. Each trial was divided, creating a case group for the combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA and control groups for each monotherapy or TAU, considered as distinct observations. Furthermore, extended or post-hoc analyses of trials were not repeatedly included in the meta-analysis; only the main trial was considered. Also, we included studies from publications that reported the same population but at different follow-up periods only once, selecting the study with the longest follow-up duration for inclusion. Trials with fewer than 50 participants per arm and those reporting outcomes solely regarding risk or hazard ratios without exact outcome figures were excluded from the meta-analysis.

Due to the number of included studies for each outcome being less than ten, funnel plots and Egger's tests were not produced to assess publication bias. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis was performed by comparing the random-effects model and the common-effects model.

Additionally, we conducted a Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) to assess the statistical robustness of the evidence provided by conventional meta-analysis (CMA) for type I or II errors. The required information size (RIS) for the interventions' effect size was determined with a type I error of 5% and a power of 90%. Effect sizes were assessed sequentially up to and including the trial that reached the RIS. From the TSA, the 95% CIs were adjusted using the alpha spending function approach to account for type I and II errors. Z-curves were calculated to compare the effectiveness of combination therapy (SGLT-2i + GLP-1RA) with GLP-1RA monotherapy, SGLT-2i monotherapy, and TAU. The Z-curves can fall into one of four categories: surpassing both the conventional and TSA thresholds (true positive, indicating the effectiveness of combination therapy), surpassing only the conventional threshold (false positive), falling below both the TSA and conventional thresholds without reaching the required sample size (false negative), and falling below both the TSA and conventional thresholds but having reached the required sample size (true negative, favoring the comparator arm). Significance testing for the TSA was conducted at the two-tailed 5% significance level. Analyses were carried out using R Statistical Software (version 4.1.1, Foundation for Statistical Computing) and TSA software (Copenhagen Trial Unit, Centre for Clinical Intervention Research, Rigs Hospitalet) [22].

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: In our study, the RoB2 tool was used to assess the quality of included studies. The majority of the studies, 25 out of 29, were assessed as having a low-risk of bias. The remaining 4 studies were rated as having some concerns regarding potential sources of bias. Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 reviewed the quality assessment of included studies. Based on GRADE assessment, the overall quality of outcomes regarding hospitalization for heart failure, safety, and metabolic outcomes associated with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA was rated as moderate. In contrast, the quality of evidence for other outcomes was deemed low. This distinction is primarily due to the moderate quality observed in the aforementioned categories, while the remaining outcomes faced issues such as inconsistency and imprecision (Supplementary Table 3).

sec.title: Cardiovascular outcomes
sec.p:
The details of the cardiovascular outcomes analysis are summarized in Table 2. For the cardiovascular outcomes, combination therapy demonstrated a significantly lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy (RR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.19; 0.75, P = 0.77, I2 = 0%; Fig. 2d), GLP-1RA monotherapy (RR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.22; 0.65, P = 0.57, I2 = 0%; Fig. 2d), and TAU (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.24; 0.75, P = 0.49, I2 = 0%; Fig. 2d). Also, the total MACE outcome showed a lower risk in the combination therapy group versus the GLP-1RA monotherapy group (RR = 0.81, 95% CI 0.65; 1.00, P = 0.90, I2 = 0%; Fig. 2a). Other comparisons, such as combination therapy versus SGLT-2i monotherapy (RR = 0.90, 95% CI 0.70; 1.12, P = 0.86, I2 = 0%, Fig. 2a) and combination therapy versus TAU (RR = 0.73, 95% CI 0.61; 0.88, P = 0.52, I2 = 0%, Fig. 2a), did not reveal any significant differences in total MACE outcomes. Regarding the cardiovascular outcomes, when examining other individual components of MACE, the analysis showed no significant differences between combination therapy and GLP-1RA monotherapy or SGLT-2i monotherapy in terms of cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, and all-cause mortality (Fig. 2).Table 2

sec.title: Metabolic and safety outcomes
sec.p:
Regarding metabolic outcomes, combination therapy demonstrated significantly greater weight loss compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy (MD = −2.20, 95% CI −3.09; −1.31, P = 0%, I2 = 100%; Fig. 3a). Additionally, combination therapy showed superior HbA1c reduction compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy (MD = -0.74, 95% CI −1.21; −0.27, P = 0, I2 = 100%, Fig. 3b). The analyses of FPG reduction did not reveal significant differences between combnation therapy and monotherapies (Fig. 3). In terms of safety outcomes, the analysis indicated a significantly higher risk of gastrointestinal adverse events, including diarrhea (RR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.10; 2.77, P = 0.59, I2 = 0%; Fig. 4d) and nausea (RR = 3.34, 95% CI 1.74; 6.43, P = 0.07, I2 = 58%; Fig. 4e), in the combination therapy group compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy. However, the incidence of other common adverse events, such as urinary tract infections, drug discontinuation due to adverse events, severe hypoglycemia, and severe adverse events, did not differ significantly between combination therapy and monotherapies (Fig. 4). sec.title: TSA analysis and sensitivity analysis
sec.p: To determine the sensitivity analysis, both random effect model and common effect model analyses were conducted for all outcomes. The comparison of these two analysis models is summarized in Supplementary Tables 4 and 5. Regarding the inclusion criteria of only including RCTs and the high heterogeneity shown in the analysis, we believe the limited number of participants may have caused bias in the results of our non-significant analysis. Therefore, we decided to conduct a TSA to determine whether sufficient participants were for the outcomes. Based on the TSA, the significant difference in the risk of hospitalization for heart failure between combination therapy and monotherapies with SGLT-2i or GLP-1RA or TAU were true positive differences, and the analysis revealed a sufficient number of participants. However, the TSA results for the all-cause mortality outcome in our study revealed an insufficient number of participants who did not reach the threshold, that may have contributed to the non-significant findings when comparing the treatment groups. The TSA results are depicted in supplementary Figs. 3–8.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the current systematic review and meta-analysis, 10 RCTs were analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA compared to monotherapy of each individually on the incidence of MACE and hospitalization for heart failure.

Our analysis showed that combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA reduced hospitalization risks for heart failure significantly more than monotherapy of each agent. A significantly lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure with combination therapy compared to monotherapy groups points to an important clinical benefit of the combined use of these medication classes. In terms of all MACE components together, we demonstrated that combination therapy was more effective than GLP-1RA monotherapy but not compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy. This reduction in the risk of total MACE events is a clinically meaningful finding as a key treatment goal for patients with T2DM, given their elevated cardiovascular disease risk.

One of the challenges of managing DM has been the lack of sufficient evidence for approving the safety and efficacy of SGLT-2is and GLP-1RAs combination therapy, as mentioned by the ESC guidelines as a knowledge gap [13]. On the other hand, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) has recommended this combination for its beneficial effect on preserving kidney function and also improving cardiovascular indexes [48]. Our results are consistent with a post hoc analysis of the EXCEL trial [29] which concluded that exenatide combined with SGLT-2i reduced the risk of MACE (defined as cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke) compared with exenatide monotherapy and also improved eGFR significantly. Cahn et al. [27] conducted a post-hoc analysis of DECLARE-TIMI 58 that enrolled 14068 participants to assess cardiorenal outcomes of dapagliflozin versus placebo in patients with T2DM by baseline use of glucose-lowering agents. Dapagliflozin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo with an additional benefit in the subgroup with baseline use of GLP-1RAs. In the AMPLITUDE-O trial [49] of 4067 participants with a median follow-up time of 1.81 years, efpeglenatide reduced major adverse cardiovascular events. Still, the long-term effects of using GLP-1RA and SGLT-2i together were unclear. Therefore, in 2022, Lam et al. [37] conducted an exploratory analysis and reported no significant differences between the effects of placebo and efpeglenatide with SGLT-2i on MACEs and hospitalizations for heart failure. However, this study didn’t evaluate GLP-1RAs other than efpeglenatide, which could affect the results. Also, Neves et al. 2023 [40] conducted a post hoc analysis of the Harmony trial evaluating the effect of albiglutide versus placebo on reducing cardiovascular events in patients with T2DM and CVD with background use of SGLT-2is. The analysis demonstrated that SGLT-2is did not modify the effect of albiglutide on reducing MACE, and the effect of albiglutide on reducing cardiovascular events was independent of SGLT-2i use. It should be noted that the small percentage of participants (6.1% in the Harmony trial) in the subgroup with baseline SGLT-2i use may have reduced the consistency of the treatment effect estimates.

In the case of all-cause mortality, a multinational cohort study with over 2 million patients with T2DM receiving insulin and a follow-up time of 5 years showed a significant reduction in all-cause mortality in those with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA combination therapy as compared to those treated with either SGLT-2i or GLP-1RA alone [50]. The discrepancy in the results between our study and this cohort could be attributed to the differences in the populations included in each investigation. The TSA conducted in our study revealed that the limited number of participants may have contributed to the non-significant findings for all-cause mortality. In contrast, this cohort study, with its larger participant numbers, provides a more robust example for assessing potential biases. However, it is important to note that the lack of randomization in observational cohort studies remains a notable limitation compared to randomized controlled trials.

Another study by Klein et al. [51] reported that combination therapy of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA showed lower odds for emergency visits, hospitalization, and mechanical ventilation among 78,806 COVID-19 patients with T2DM compared to monotherapy. Among other glucose-lowering agents added to GLP-1RA, a propensity score-matched cohort study [52] demonstrated a meaningful reduction in heart failure hospitalization in those with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA compared to those taking a combination of sulfonylurea medications and GLP-1RA.

It seems that SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA exert their cardiovascular benefits through complementary mechanisms. SGLT-2is improve ventricular preload through natriuresis and osmotic diuresis, decreasing blood pressure and reducing afterload. These agents also enhance cardiac metabolism by using ketones instead of glucose. In addition, SGLT-2is contribute to better cardiovascular outcomes by stimulating erythropoiesis (leading to improved oxygenation of ischemic tissues), reducing proinflammatory adipokines, and reducing cardiac necrosis [16, 53–56]. Compared to SGLT-2is, GLP1-RAs appear to exert cardiovascular benefits through their anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and anti-atherogenic properties [16, 55–59]. As discussed, SGLT-2is and GLP-1RAs concomitant therapy may produce additive cardiovascular benefits.

Recent studies have examined the cost–benefit tradeoffs associated with using newer diabetes medications in combination with standard therapies. One study found that patients who added SGLT-2i to their existing diabetes regimen experienced an average monthly cost-saving of 75.7 Euros due to reduced incidence of MACE [60]. Another related study reported incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of 23717 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained for SGLT-2i and 100705 per QALY gained for GLP-1RA [61]. Additionally, accessibility challenges associated with GLP-1RA can complicate their integration into treatment regimens in many countries. Many patients face barriers such as high out-of-pocket costs and limited insurance coverage for these medications, which can hinder adherence and ultimately affect treatment outcomes [62]. Understanding the economic implications and addressing the accessibility issues of combination therapy is crucial, especially as healthcare systems aim to optimize resource allocation while enhancing patient care. Future research should focus on comprehensive cost-effectiveness analyses that compare the long-term benefits of combination therapy against traditional monotherapies, considering not only direct medical costs but also potential savings from decreased hospitalizations and improved quality of life.

Our results suggest that combination therapy leads to a greater reduction in body weight, HbA1c, and FPG compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy. The greater reduction in body weight and HbA1c levels compared to SGLT-2i monotherapy and TAU are noteworthy, as achieving optimal glycemic control and weight management are central to diabetes management. The superior FPG lowering with combination therapy versus GLP-1RA is also clinically relevant. In line with our results, a systematic review and meta-analysis by Li et al. [63] encompassing 1895 patients with T2DM reported a greater reduction in HbA1c, body weight, FPG, systolic blood pressure, BMI, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in a combination therapy group, compared to monotherapy with either GLP-1RA or SGLT-2i. These findings are supported by the studies of Jabbour et al. [36] and Ludvik et al. [9] comparing patients using exenatide plus dapagliflozin and dulaglutide plus SGLT-2i with placebo, respectively. Moreover, Zinman et al. [11] showed a greater reduction in body weight and HbA1c in patients using semaglutide plus SGLT-2i in comparison with monotherapy. Other trials also reported a reduction in body weight, HbA1c, and FPG in patients receiving combination therapy with SGLT-2i plus GLP-1RA [9, 23, 46]. The effect of combination therapy on body weight might be explained by the effects on brain centers that control energy balance, contributing to increased appetite in response to SGLT-2i and decreased food intake with GLP-1RA [45]. The reduction in blood pressure after receiving SGLT-2i is also caused by the effect of these drugs on natriuresis, osmotic diuresis, and regulation of the autonomic nervous system [64]. Although the mentioned studies used different drugs from SGLT-2i or GLP-RA groups, they reported the same results, which explains how combination therapy with SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA can improve outcomes, regardless of the specific drug.

Previous reviews of clinical trials evaluated the effect of the SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA combination on metabolic factors, and they showed a mostly positive effect [65, 66]. However, there has been inconsistencies between their results. Guo et al., in a systematic review and meta-analysis including five RCTs and 1604 participants, showed the efficacy and safety of this combination in the reduction of fasting plasma glucose (FPG) level, and 2 h postprandial (2-HPP) glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c), and systolic blood pressure (SBP) [66]. On the other hand, Tuersun et al. meta-analysis showed the superiority of the mentioned combination on SGLT-2is monotherapy regarding the control of HbA1c, FPG, and SBP. Both studies showed no increase in the adverse effects of combining these two medication groups [65]. The same positive effect on lipid profile indices, blood glucose, and weight management has been shown by another meta-analysis with four RCTs included [67]. It should be noted that these two reviews did not provide an analysis and conclusion regarding the effect of combination therapy on major cardiovascular events. The present study has evaluated these clinically crucial factors and provided the data regarding them individually and as a composite (MACE).

The risk of adverse gastrointestinal events of combination therapy versus monotherapy of either SGLT-2i or GLP-1RA, including nausea and diarrhea, was significantly higher in our meta-analysis. Regarding safety, the increased gastrointestinal side effects of combination therapy are not unexpected, given the known profiles of the individual medication classes. However, the lack of significant difference in other common adverse events suggests the combination may be well-tolerated overall. Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events in the study by Zinman et al. [11], comparing semaglutide plus SGLT-2i with placebo. Patients using combination therapy have been shown to report diarrhea and nausea at a higher rate than patients receiving a placebo [36].

Other adverse events investigated in our study were urinary tract infections (UTI), drug discontinuation due to adverse events, severe hypoglycemia, and other severe adverse events, which showed no significant difference between groups. This finding aligns with the results of Guo et al.'s study, which showed no significant increase in the combination group’s incidence of clinically considerable adverse effects such as hypoglycemia or urinary infections [66]. Jabbour et al. [36, 37] reported UTI as the most common adverse event in their trial. Hypoglycemia is another commonly reported event after combination therapy [9, 42]. Additionally, serious adverse events requiring emergent treatment, such as hypersensitivity reactions, occurred at a higher rate in patients receiving combination therapy [9, 26]. These studies have mentioned limitations such as short trial durations and small populations, which might explain their different results.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the MACE and hospitalization for heart failure outcomes of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA combination therapy and its metabolic and safety outcomes. All the articles included in our analysis had combination therapy as a category of cases, and we had a detailed number of events for each outcome analysis. In contrast, other similar studies used hazard ratios for their analysis or utilized network analysis methods to compare combination therapy versus monotherapies. Furthermore, outcomes such as mortality and myocardial infarction were not sufficiently examined. By TAS analysis, we found that all other outcomes, except hospitalization for heart failure, did not have enough or sufficient population. Additionally, the study population was relatively small, and the number of included studies was limited. This precluded the ability to conduct robust subgroup analyses comparing the different medications within the SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA classes. Furthermore, the definition of MACE varied among the included studies, potentially introducing the bias; however, the most commonly used definition in our included studies was components of MI, stroke, and CV death or all-cause mortality. We acknowledge that our inclusion of heart failure patients irrespective of their left ventiruclar ejection fraction (LVEF) is a limitation, as LVEF may not always be reported consistently across studies. Further research is needed to directly assess the comparative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of combination therapy using each drug class individually, including the newer agents, semaglutide and tirzepatide. This is of interest given that the current review included only one study evaluating semaglutide, which showed significantly greater weight reduction compared with other GLP-1RA. Moreover, as a systematic study, there might be publication bias, which could have influenced our results. To avoid a similar population adding to the analysis, we included the trial with the longest follow-up period in our analysis among the studies with the same population but various follow-up periods. However, the wide range of study follow-up periods prohibited a subgroup analysis. Subgroup analysis based on the dosage of drugs could not be done for the same reason mentioned for the follow-up period. Due to a limited number of studies and incomplete information about drug dosages, we could not determine specific dosages and categorize them.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The findings demonstrate that the combination of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA holds substantial promise for improving cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes in patients with T2DM. The observed reduction in total MACE and lower risk of heart failure hospitalization provides encouraging evidence that combination therapy may meaningfully reduce cardiovascular disease burden in this high-risk population. Additionally, the greater reductions in body weight, HbA1c, and FPG with combination therapy versus monotherapies further underscore its potential to optimize glycemic control and weight management, which are cornerstones of comprehensive diabetes care. While increased gastrointestinal side effects were noted, the overall tolerability appears acceptable. To build on these promising results, future research should focus on evaluating the safety and efficacy of this combination, particularly as newer incretin-based therapies emerge. Larger cardiovascular outcomes trials and studies on diabetes-related microvascular complications will help solidify the role of this approach in future diabetes management guidelines. These findings generate excitement for improving long-term outcomes for individuals living with T2DM.
